name: Propofol
route_note: IV bolus for induction and continuous infusion (including target-controlled infusion) for maintenance and sedation.
targets: GABA-A receptors (positive allosteric modulator, beta subunits)

discovery.by: John B. Glen and Roger James (ICI Pharmaceuticals)
discovery.note: Identified among alkylphenols screened for hypnotic activity in animals; first human trial in 1977 in Cremophor EL, later reformulated in a soybean oil emulsion.

tagline: Milky white IV anaesthetic with rapid onset and clear-headed recovery
summary: Propofol is the most widely used intravenous anaesthetic, given to induce and maintain general anaesthesia and for sedation in intensive care and procedures. It acts within a minute, wears off quickly with little hangover and reduces nausea, but it causes dose-dependent respiratory depression and hypotension and requires airway expertise.
mechanism: Propofol potentiates GABA-A receptors by binding at sites involving the beta subunits, prolonging chloride channel opening; at higher concentrations it directly activates the receptor. Enhanced inhibition in cortical, thalamic and brainstem arousal networks produces unconsciousness.
Its high lipid solubility allows rapid entry into the brain and quick redistribution, explaining fast onset and recovery. It is formulated as a lipid emulsion because it is nearly insoluble in water.
uses: Induction and maintenance of general anaesthesia
Sedation of ventilated adults in intensive care

history.title: Discovery
history.detail: John Glen and Roger James identify propofol at ICI.

history.title: First human trial
history.detail: Kay and Rolly report clinical use in a Cremophor EL formulation, later withdrawn because of anaphylactoid reactions.

history.title: Launch
history.detail: The reformulated lipid emulsion is launched in the UK as Diprivan.

history.title: FDA approval
history.detail: Diprivan is approved in the US.

history.title: Propofol infusion syndrome
history.detail: Reports describe deaths in children sedated with prolonged propofol infusions.

history.title: Additive
history.detail: Disodium edetate is added to the US formulation to limit microbial growth.

history.title: Michael Jackson
history.detail: The singer's death from propofol intoxication outside a medical setting draws attention to its misuse.

history.title: Lasker Award
history.detail: John Glen receives the Lasker–DeBakey Clinical Medical Research Award for discovering propofol.

pk.half_life: Distribution 2–8 minutes; terminal 4–7 hours (context-sensitive half-time short)
pk.metabolism: Hepatic glucuronidation and CYP2B6 hydroxylation; extrahepatic metabolism

serious: Propofol infusion syndrome (metabolic acidosis, rhabdomyolysis, cardiac failure)

facts: Propofol emulsion supports bacterial growth, so strict aseptic handling and limits on open time are required.
